vignette:
He sits in his corner office on the twenty-second floor, the afternoon sun glinting off the harbor. The city spreads out below him—ferries cutting white lines across the blue, cranes swinging over the port. He has been a publisher for thirty-seven years, long enough to have printed the stories of a thousand others, but now he cannot read a single page of his own life. His hands rest on the desk, still as stone, though inside his chest something trembles.

Five years ago, during the annual island festival, he stood with his wife on a newly built grandstand. The wood was still pale, the nails bright. A local band was playing, and the crowd—hundreds of families—clapped in rhythm. The structure groaned once, then twice, then the world split. He remembers the sound: not a crack but a deep, wet snap, like a palm tree giving way in a storm. The platform tilted, and people slid. He grabbed his wife’s arm, pulled her toward the edge, and they fell together onto the grass. Behind him, the grandstand folded like a cardboard box. Dust, screams, a child’s shoe lying on its side. He helped a woman with a broken leg, then another, then his hands were covered in someone else’s blood, and he could not stop shaking.

The disaster was man-made—the builders had used untreated timber, the bolts were undersized, the permits were rushed. Twelve people died. Thirty more were injured. He was one of the lucky ones, the papers said. He even wrote a front-page editorial calling for accountability. But the words came from a place that was already crumbling.

Now he rarely takes the ferry. He drives instead, even though the traffic costs him an hour each day. The ferry dock smells like salt and diesel, and when the horn sounds, his throat closes. He cannot watch people line up at the railing. His wife has learned to book appointments on the mainland only when he is away. She does not complain. At night, he wakes drenched, the dream always the same: he is under the grandstand, pinned, and no one hears him. He does not scream out loud anymore. He lies still, counting her breaths until the shaking stops.

At work, his editorial meetings have become unbearable. He cancels them, sends emails instead. His assistant brings him manuscripts about hurricanes, courtroom dramas, survival stories. He cannot finish them. The latest is a memoir by a woman who escaped a burning building, and he has been editing the same sentence for three weeks: *I ran because the fire was behind me.* He wants to write in the margin, *But what if the fire is inside?* Instead, he closes the file.

He has not attended a festival since. Not a parade, not a school play, not even the book launch for his own anniversary edition. He tells people he is busy, but his wife knows. She finds him standing in the dark hallway at 3 a.m., staring at a framed photograph of the island before the fall. He does not turn on the light.

Yesterday, walking home from the station, a delivery truck backfired. He dropped his briefcase, spun around, and crouched behind a mailbox. A teenager on a skateboard laughed. His wife, who had been waiting at the gate, ran to him. She put her hand on his shoulder, and he flinched—not from her, but from the memory of the wood snapping. He whispered, “I’m sorry.” She said nothing, just held him until his heart slowed.

In the morning, he will go back to the office. He will stare at the harbor. He will open the manuscript and read the same line again. The work of words is all he knows. But the story he carries has no ending, and he is still inside it.
